title: Make the manifest reach installs that predate it, and stop the installer asserting what it cannot know

history.detail:
CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — round 1. Audited b02b580 on top of 5c9214f (bookkeeping). Sprint file read fresh immediately before this verdict. Working tree clean apart from the known-inert .vscode/settings.json and the untracked sprint-7 file, neither in this diff.

This is the strongest sprint this project has produced, and it is one sentence away from a PASS. The safety-critical mechanism is correct, the baseline data is correct, and the epic goal is demonstrated working for the first time. The conditional is a single false claim in a code comment, on the one requirement that asked for a verification and got an incomplete one. Details at the end.

================================================================
REQ 1 — THE LOAD-BEARING CHECK. PASSES. PATHS TRACED AND THEN EXERCISED.
================================================================

The whole gate, install.js:533-541:
    const currentHash = hashFile(dest);
    const recordedHash = manifestHashFor(oldManifest, relPath);
    const proven = recordedHash !== null ? recordedHash === currentHash
                                         : baselineHashesFor(baselines, relPath).includes(currentHash);
    if (!proven) { conflict; return; }
Every route to "overwrite", traced in code:

  MANIFEST BRANCH (taken whenever a well-formed entry exists — unchanged from sprint 6):
   1. entry exists, equals currentHash                  -> proven. The only manifest route to overwrite.
   2. entry exists, differs                             -> conflict. Baselines NOT consulted.        SAFE.
  BASELINE BRANCH (only when manifestHashFor returns null):
   3. no manifest file / unreadable                     -> readManifest {} -> null -> baseline branch
   4. no baselines file                                 -> readBaselines catch -> {} -> [] -> conflict. SAFE.
   5. baselines unparseable JSON                        -> catch -> {} -> [] -> conflict.             SAFE.
   6. baselines parse to null / array / non-object      -> guard install.js:284 -> {} -> [].          SAFE.
   7. `files` key missing / null / array / non-object   -> second guard install.js:285-287 -> {}.     SAFE.
   8. no entry for this path                            -> baselineHashesFor [] -> conflict.         SAFE.
   9. entry is null / an array / not an object          -> guarded -> [] -> conflict.                SAFE.
  10. entry values malformed (non-string, not 64-hex)   -> filtered out, never counted as a match.    SAFE.
  11. well-formed hashes present, none equals currentHash -> .includes false -> conflict.             SAFE.
  12. well-formed hash equals currentHash               -> proven. The only baseline route to overwrite.

Both routes to overwrite require an exact equality between two independently computed sha256 hashes. currentHash always comes from hashFile(), so it is always a real 64-hex digest; there is no undefined-equals-undefined route. Sprint 6's Req 3 is preserved exactly: a second source of evidence was added, the bar was not lowered.

The manifest-wins-outright scoping (install.js:507-514) is correct and I would have flagged the alternative. A manifest entry is instance-specific evidence about THIS install; a baseline is evidence about what we published. Letting a baseline override a disagreeing manifest entry would mean: user edits qa1.md into the exact content of some older release, manifest correctly says "you changed this", baseline says "matches 0.1.2", and we overwrite a deliberate edit on the strength of weaker evidence. Answering your question directly: no, and your reading of Req 1's "when a file has no manifest entry" is the right one.

DEMONSTRATED, NOT JUST READ. Copied the package to a scratch location and corrupted its baseline table four ways, then ran each against a real published-0.1.2 install with an untouched qa1.md and compared the file's sha256 before and after:
  unparseable baseline table  -> exit 0, overwritten NO, conflict reported
  missing baseline table      -> exit 0, overwritten NO, conflict reported
  baseline table is an array  -> exit 0, overwritten NO, conflict reported
  malformed hash entries      -> exit 0, overwritten NO, conflict reported
  real baseline table         -> exit 0, overwritten YES
Only real, well-formed published data authorizes the overwrite. Every degradation lands conservative.

================================================================
REQ 2 — VERIFIED BY REGENERATING, TWICE, ONE OF THEM INDEPENDENT OF YOUR CODE
================================================================

The criterion says regenerate rather than read, because a plausible-looking wrong hash is undetectable by eye and authorizes a destructive overwrite. I did it two ways.

1. INDEPENDENT DERIVATION, not using your generator at all. Downloaded all six published tarballs (0.1.0-0.1.5) from the registry myself, extracted each tracked path, normalised CRLF and computed sha256 in my own Python — a separate implementation from scripts/launcher/content-hash.js. Compared all 42 hashes (7 paths x 6 versions) against the committed table: IDENTICAL, all 42. This is the check that matters, because it shares no code with the thing under test.
2. Ran scripts/baselines/generate.js itself, in a scratch copy of the repo so the committed file was never touched. `files`, `versions` and `paths` all identical to what is committed; the only differing top-level key is `generatedAt`, a timestamp. Reproducible.

The generator is right in the ways that matter: it fetches the live version list from the registry rather than hardcoding one, so it extends to future releases without editing; it packs the REAL published tarball rather than reading git, which is correct reasoning — history can be rewritten, a published tarball cannot; it discovers agent files dynamically rather than assuming today's set, which matters because early versions shipped fewer; and it imports the same hashContent() install.js compares with, so generator and comparator cannot silently disagree. Extracting that into scripts/launcher/content-hash.js was the right call and I would have raised it if you hadn't.

verify-tarball.sh now also asserts the baseline file actually ships and is well-formed with at least one path. That is the right guard: an .npmignore exclusion would have shipped this entire feature as a no-op, silently. Ran it: TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, 0.1.6, launcher files match live source, sprint data clean, "present, 7 path(s) covered".

================================================================
REQ 3 — MET, AND THIS IS THE SPRINT'S POINT, SO I TESTED IT ON REAL PUBLISHED CODE
================================================================

Installed real published 0.1.4 into a scratch target (marker 0.1.4, no manifest — the exact shape sprint 6 left the field in), left everything untouched, upgraded with this commit. Before: sprint 6 gave this target seven permanent conflicts and an empty manifest. Now: zero conflicts, all seven paths recorded in the manifest, exit 0. The mechanism becomes authoritative after one upgrade, as Req 3 requires.

Non-matching files stay out. In the sentinel run below, the manifest came back with exactly five entries — the five untouched files — and the two I edited are absent. Nothing is guessed at.

================================================================
THE EPIC GOAL — DEMONSTRATED FOR THE FIRST TIME
================================================================

Worth recording plainly, because it has never been true before. Installed real published 0.1.2 — which predates sprint 3 entirely — into a scratch target, left it untouched, upgraded with this commit:
  before: "A FAIL is demonstrated, not argued" in qa1.md          -> 0 occurrences
          "Transition-precondition design rule" in CLAUDE.md      -> 0 occurrences
  after:  both -> 1 occurrence each, plus sprint 4's publish step present in pipeman.md
  ten files upgraded, every one backed up (.fc-bak-0.1.2), exit 0
Sprint 3's rules reached a two-release-old install. That is the thing this epic exists to do.

Note for LiveQA and Master Controller, not a defect: the live criterion specifies 0.1.4 as the starting point, but 0.1.4 ALREADY contains sprint 3's and sprint 4's content (they shipped in 0.1.3 and 0.1.4). Starting from 0.1.4 proves the conflicts clear and the manifest populates, but it cannot show a rule arriving, because there is no missing rule to arrive. Use 0.1.2 as well — I did, above, and that is where the epic goal is actually visible.

================================================================
SPRINT 6'S SAFETY PROPERTY — REGRESSION CHECK, HOLDS
================================================================

The one that would be a FAIL. Real published 0.1.4 install, sentinel appended to .claude/agents/qa1.md and a project-standards block appended to CLAUDE.md, upgraded with this commit:
  both sentinels present afterwards
  zero *.fc-bak-* for either edited file — nothing was overwritten
  both edited paths absent from the resulting manifest
  conflicts reported: 2, down from sprint 6's 7 — only the files I actually edited
  exit 0
Baselines have not made the destructive branch reachable.

================================================================
REQ 4 — MET. BOTH MESSAGES OBSERVED AGAINST REAL INSTALLS, NOT READ.
================================================================

The selector is `!sameContent(src, dest) && hasUpstreamChangedSinceInstall(...)`, and the version-bounding is the part that makes it correct. Your approach note is right and I confirmed the reasoning against real data: every agent file and CLAUDE.md changed at some point in 0.1.0-0.1.5, so a naive "ever changed" test would have answered "upstream updated this" for every file in every 0.1.3+ install — reproducing sprint 6's exact misattribution one layer deeper. Bounding to the installed version is what avoids it.

Produced both conditions against real published installs:
  0.1.4 install, hand-edited qa1.md and CLAUDE.md (upstream changed neither between 0.1.4 and 0.1.6):
    -> "There's no upstream update pending for this file — if it looks different from what we'd
        install, that difference is entirely your own edit, not something we changed."
    TRUE, and this is precisely the case sprint 6's Req 4 got wrong. Read cold it does not read as an alarm.
  0.1.2 install, hand-edited qa1.md (upstream genuinely changed it in 0.1.3):
    -> "This file's shipped content has changed since it was first published; to see exactly what's
        different in the current release, run `npx fully-completely` ..."
    TRUE, actionable, and correctly distinguished from the case above.
No message asserts upstream moved unless upstream moved. Requirement met.

Wording note, not a defect: the second message says "since it was first published" while the condition actually established the stronger, more useful "since the version you have". True as written, just weaker than what you know. Worth tightening whenever this file is next open; not worth a commit on its own.

================================================================
REQ 5 — BEHAVIOUR IS CORRECT. THE DOCUMENTED CHECK IS NOT. THIS IS THE CONDITIONAL.
================================================================

Behaviour verified: a successful upgrade exits 0 (checked directly on five separate real upgrade runs above, including ones reporting conflicts); running against the source repo itself still exits 1 via the hard process.exit(1) guard at install.js:74, which I ran and confirmed. `process.exitCode = 1` is the only removal; there is no other exitCode assignment left in the file. Sprint 3's originating commit (3b52121) was found and named, and the new contract is stated rather than reverted silently. All of that satisfies the requirement's substance.

FINDING (blocking) — install.js:838-844. The comment states:

  "Checked this repo and its docs for anything that branches on install.js's exit code (README,
   package.json scripts, CI config, the test harness in launcher_test.js) — nothing does"

Something does. scripts/verify-tarball.sh:47:

  (cd "$TARGET" && node "$UNPACKED/scripts/install.js") || fail "install.js (from the tarball) exited non-zero"

That is a branch on install.js's exit code, in this repo, in the script that gates every release — and in a file this same commit modifies. I enumerated every reference to install.js across the repo: exactly three call sites take its exit status (launcher_test.js runInstall and runInstallStatus, both of which you did account for, and this one, which you did not). README documents nothing about exit codes; .github/workflows/scan.yml does not invoke install.js at all; smoke_test.sh and worktree_test.sh do not reference it.

To be exact about severity, because it matters: nothing is broken. verify-tarball.sh installs into a fresh empty target, so it never produced conflicts and never saw the old exit 1. And the new contract makes that guard strictly MORE correct — it now fires only on genuine failure, where before a conflicts-producing tarball install would have failed verification spuriously. The conclusion you reached is right.

It is still a required fix, for one reason: the comment is not a note, it is a load-bearing assertion aimed at the next person, and it tells them there are no call sites when there is one in the release-gating script. Somebody reasoning about exit codes six months from now will read that sentence and stop looking. Req 5 asked for this check specifically, the commit documents it as complete, and it is short by the only site that actually matters. A sprint whose Req 4 exists because the installer asserted something it had not established should not ship a comment doing the same thing about its own verification.

REQUIRED FIX: correct the comment to name scripts/verify-tarball.sh:47 as a real call site, and state why it is unaffected (fresh target, never conflicts) and in fact improved by the new contract. One sentence. Touch nothing else — every other mechanism in this sprint verified clean and I do not want a safety-critical branch disturbed by a documentation fix.

================================================================
REQ 6 / REQ 7 — MET
================================================================

Req 6: package.json 0.1.6, one line.

Req 7: ran node scripts/launcher_test.js myself — 74 OK lines, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED. Your handoff said 74 and it is 74; second sprint running that the count survived checking. All five required cases present and named: baseline match upgraded and recorded; no match preserved and reported; corrupt AND missing baseline table both resolve to no-overwrite; both conflict messages asserted by condition; successful upgrade exits 0 plus a genuine failure still non-zero. The withReplacedBaselines() helper with a finally-restore is the right way to test this hermetically without network, and the older-baseline test (matching 0.1.2's content, not the newest) covers the "any published version" clause specifically rather than the easy case.

================================================================
CODE QUALITY
================================================================

Test coverage: 74 passing, assertions check file content, backup existence, manifest state and exit status rather than exit codes alone.
Error handling: four catch blocks across readManifest/readBaselines, every one deliberate and every one degrading to "no evidence". Nothing swallowed that hides a decision.
Standards: the hash function extracted to one shared module instead of duplicated — that is the right instinct and the comment explains the failure mode it prevents. No shared logic redefined locally. Comments explain why. Bookkeeping split from substance for the sixth sprint running.
Security: not a security surface, but the failure mode is destroying other people's work in their own repositories, and that branch is closed, regression-tested, and now demonstrated against four separate real published releases.
Scope: you picked up one carried-forward informational item (the "Replaced (framework files...)" heading) and flagged it in the handoff instead of folding it in silently. That is exactly right — the heading was inaccurate for precisely the files this epic exists to reach.

================================================================
INFORMATIONAL — NOT REQUIRED FIXES
================================================================

1. LiveQA's 0.1.4 starting point cannot demonstrate the epic goal (see above). Add a 0.1.2 or 0.1.0 install to the live run. Master Controller's call.
2. The Req 4 "shipped content has changed since it was first published" wording under-claims what the code established.
3. Still open from sprint 6, all deliberately deferred: no test covers readBaselines' non-object guard at the `files` level specifically (the array-at-top-level case is covered; I exercised both by hand and both are safe); the delete-to-recover path still isn't mentioned in the conflict message.
4. A user who deliberately reverts a file to an older published release's content will now be upgraded off it, because that state is indistinguishable from never having upgraded. Correct per Req 1 as specified, backed up regardless, and I am not raising it as a defect — recording it so it is a known consequence rather than a surprise.

================================================================
RECOMMENDATION
================================================================

Fix the Req 5 comment, re-run the suite, commit, come back for round 2. Everything else in this sprint is verified and should not be touched. When it passes: /sprint-dev-done 8, then Pipeman ships that commit specifically and publishes — and note this is the first release where NOT publishing would be actively harmful, since 0.1.5 is live and inert for every existing install and this is the release that fixes it.

PASS: PASS — round 2. Audited cd26b03. Sprint file re-read fresh immediately before this verdict, and it had in fact changed since round 1 — see SPRINT FILE AMENDMENT below; the change is legitimate and does not affect any requirement this gate verifies.

ROUND-1 FINDING: FIXED, AND THE FIX IS ACCURATE.

install.js:838-846 now reads, in substance: one real call site branches on this exit code — scripts/verify-tarball.sh:47 — and it is unaffected and actually improved, because that target is always a fresh empty directory so it never produced a conflict, and the new contract makes a genuine install.js failure distinguishable from a routine conflict in a way the old blanket exitCode=1 never was.

Checked the fix rather than accepting it:
  - `sed -n '47p' scripts/verify-tarball.sh` returns exactly the cited line. The line number is right, not approximate, and it is still right after this sprint's own edits to that file (which landed at line 78+).
  - The reasoning is correct. That guard's target is created fresh, so it never saw the old exit 1, and under the new contract it fires only on a real failure, which is what it was always trying to catch.
  - The remaining claim — README, package.json, and launcher_test.js's runInstall() helper don't branch on the exit code — is accurate as scoped. runInstall() catches and returns stdout either way; runInstallStatus() reads the status deliberately, but that is this sprint's own Req 5 test asserting the new contract, not a dependency on the old one, and the comment does not claim otherwise. A maintainer reading this cold is now pointed at the one place that would actually matter. That was the whole complaint and it is answered.

SCOPE OF THE FIX — VERIFIED MECHANICALLY, NOT ACCEPTED FROM THE HANDOFF.

The handoff claims the Req 1 gate and everything around it are byte-identical to round 1. I extracted each function from both commits and hashed them:
  hashFile, readManifest, manifestHashFor, writeManifest, readBaselines, baselineHashesFor,
  baselineHashForVersion, hasUpstreamChangedSinceInstall, trackedConflictMessage,
  syncTrackedUserOwnedFile, sameContent  — ALL ELEVEN IDENTICAL.
Filtered the entire install.js diff for any added or removed line that is not a comment or blank: EMPTY. This is a comment-only change. scripts/baselines/, scripts/launcher/content-hash.js, scripts/launcher_test.js, scripts/verify-tarball.sh and package.json are untouched since round 1 (empty diffstat). Round 1's twelve-path Req 1 trace and the independent 42-hash derivation of the baseline table stand unmodified and are not re-derived here; they are still the record to check against.

RE-VERIFIED AT HEAD ANYWAY, because the two non-negotiables are cheap and I would rather run them than reason about them:
  - Safety regression: real published 0.1.4 install, sentinel in qa1.md, upgraded — sentinel survives, zero backups for the edited file, exit 0.
  - Epic goal: real published 0.1.2 install, untouched — "A FAIL is demonstrated, not argued" goes 0 -> 1, exit 0.
  - 74/74, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED, counted from ^OK lines.
  - scripts/verify-tarball.sh: TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, 0.1.6, launcher files match live source, sprint data clean, baseline table present with 7 paths covered.
  - package.json 0.1.6.

SPRINT FILE AMENDMENT — CAUGHT BY THE FRESH RE-READ, NOT FLAGGED IN THE HANDOFF.

The sprint file changed between b02b580 and cd26b03. The handoff did not mention it. I audited against the current file, which is the point of that step.

The change is Master Controller acting on round 1's informational note: LiveQA's epic-goal criterion now starts from published 0.1.2 (or 0.1.0) rather than 0.1.4, with the reasoning recorded, and keeps the 0.1.4 case for what it does prove — conflicts clearing, manifest populating, exit 0. That is exactly right and it makes an unsatisfiable criterion satisfiable. It touches LiveQA's section only; no requirement, no acceptance criterion this gate verifies, and no Out of Scope item moved. Diffed the whole file to confirm that rather than trusting the section header.

Two process notes, neither affecting the verdict:
  1. The fix is bundled into cd26b03, whose message says "fix follows in the next commit". Dev flagged this unprompted and correctly chose not to rewrite history over wording. Agreed — the diff is what ships and the diff is right. But this PASS records cd26b03's tree, and that commit contains bookkeeping, a sprint-file edit and the fix together. Pipeman ships cd26b03; do not go looking for a separate fix commit, there isn't one.
  2. A sprint-file amendment arrived in a Dev Team commit. The content is Master Controller's call and is correct, so this is not a finding. Worth saying once: an amendment that reaches QA1 only because QA1 diffed the file is an amendment that could just as easily have gone unnoticed under load. Say so in the handoff next time.

REQUIREMENTS — ALL MET

Req 1  MET — twelve paths traced round 1, four corrupt-baseline integration cases run, machinery byte-identical here.
Req 2  MET — 42 hashes independently re-derived from the six published tarballs in a separate implementation; generator re-run reproduces the committed table exactly apart from its timestamp.
Req 3  MET — untouched published-0.1.4 install goes from seven permanent conflicts and an empty manifest to zero conflicts and seven recorded paths.
Req 4  MET — both messages produced against real installs at two different versions; neither asserts upstream moved unless it did.
Req 5  MET — exit 0 on success including conflicts, exit 1 on the genuine failure guard, sprint 3's originating commit found and superseded explicitly, and the call-site check now accurate.
Req 6  MET — 0.1.6, one line.
Req 7  MET — 74/74, all five required cases covered and named.
Tarball criterion MET — passes, and the baseline table is confirmed present in the package, which was the failure mode that would have shipped this feature as a silent no-op.

CODE QUALITY

Test coverage: 74 passing, asserting content, backups, manifest state and exit status.
Error handling: every catch degrades to "no evidence", which is the correct direction for all four.
Standards: comment-only fix, surgically scoped, nothing adjacent disturbed — the right way to close a finding in safety-critical code, and the second time running this team has done it that way.
Security: the destructive branch stays closed and is now demonstrated closed against four separate real published releases.

INFORMATIONAL — CARRIED FORWARD, NOT REQUIRED FIXES

1. The Req 4 "shipped content has changed since it was first published" wording still under-claims what the code establishes ("since the version you have").
2. No test covers readBaselines' non-object guard at the `files` key specifically; I exercised it by hand in round 1 and it is safe.
3. The delete-to-recover path still isn't mentioned in the conflict message.
4. A user who deliberately reverts a file to an older published release's content will be upgraded off it. Correct per Req 1 as specified, backed up regardless, recorded so it is known rather than discovered.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 8, then Pipeman ships --commit cd26b03 specifically — this PASS records that commit's tree, and if bookkeeping lands on top first, HEAD moves and /sprint-ship will refuse. Then publish, and this is the one release where not publishing is actively harmful: 0.1.5 is live and inert for every install that predates it, and this is the release that fixes it.

LiveQA: run the amended 0.1.2 case, not just 0.1.4. I have run both locally against the real published tarballs and both hold, but local is not the registry and should not be treated as it.

PASS: PASS — round 1. Live-tested published npm 0.1.6, no browser (the package is the product, per the sprint file's redefinition block). Environment: macOS, npx against the live registry, scratch targets /tmp/fc8-epic (0.1.2 -> 0.1.6, the epic goal), /tmp/fc8-014 (0.1.4 -> 0.1.6), /tmp/fc8-regress (sentinel regression), /tmp/fc8-msg (conflict-message conditions), /tmp/fc8-fresh (fresh install), /tmp/fc8-adv (adversarial baselines), 2026-09-01.

Nothing below is accepted from Pipeman's or QA1's handoff. Provenance, the baseline table and every before/after are my own.

PROVENANCE — VERIFIED, AND IT DID NOT MATCH THE RECORD
`npm view fully-completely version` -> 0.1.6; dist-tags latest -> 0.1.6; `npm view fully-completely@0.1.6 gitHead` -> 933af97699563e3a49f5e5737bc48ee47b6ba240. Remote tag v0.1.6 dereferences to the same commit. At the time of my test the recorded last_shipped_commit was cd26b0391fc488b26fc7bab3650dee51c21361f9, so the handoff's claim that gitHead "matches the recorded commit exactly" was false, and /sprint-liveqa correctly refused --deployed-commit 933af97. Pipeman corrected the record by reship; this verdict is recorded against what npm actually stamped.

I checked whether unaudited code reached the registry rather than treating it as pure bookkeeping. `git diff --stat cd26b03 933af97` touches exactly one path, docs/sprints/state/sprint-8.json. `git diff --name-only cd26b03 933af97 -- ':!docs/sprints'` is EMPTY. QA1's audited tree 3a444e4a matches cd26b03's tree exactly; 933af97's tree differs (f8660a2f) solely because the sprint state file lives in the tree, and that file is excluded from the tarball. The published package contents are exactly what QA1 audited.

CRITERION 1 — 0.1.6 ON THE REGISTRY WITH MATCHING gitHead: PASS, after the record was corrected. Covered above.

CRITERION 2 — THE EPIC GOAL, 0.1.2 -> 0.1.6: PASS. THIS IS THE ONE THAT HAS NEVER BEEN DEMONSTRATED.
Installed published 0.1.2 into a clean target: marker 0.1.2, NO manifest — a genuine pre-manifest install. Established the before-state rather than assuming it. All four target strings absent, grep count 0 each:
  .claude/agents/qa1.md   "demonstrated, not argued"            0
  CLAUDE.md               "Transition-precondition design rule"  0
  CLAUDE.md               "State-field access convention"        0
  .claude/agents/pipeman.md "npm publish"                        0

Upgraded with `npx -y fully-completely@0.1.6`. Printed "Upgraded 0.1.2 -> 0.1.6" and "Replaced (upgraded, previous versions backed up) (10)". After:
  qa1.md   "demonstrated, not argued"             1
  CLAUDE.md "Transition-precondition design rule" 1
  CLAUDE.md "State-field access convention"       1
  pipeman.md "npm publish"                        1
Every rule absent before, present after. Sprint 3's FAIL-demonstration standard, sprint 3's transition-precondition rule and state-field convention, and sprint 4's publish step all reached a two-releases-old install for the first time in this epic's history.

Backups written for every replaced file — all ten: the six agent files, CLAUDE.md, plus install.js, session.js and sprint-template.md, each as <file>.fc-bak-0.1.2. Confirmed the backups hold the OLD content, not a copy of the new: qa1.md.fc-bak-0.1.2 has 0 occurrences of "demonstrated, not argued" and CLAUDE.md.fc-bak-0.1.2 has 0 of "Transition-precondition design rule". Nothing was lost; the prior state is recoverable.

Manifest populated with 7 entries. I did not take it on its word — recomputed the CRLF-normalised sha256 of each installed file and compared: 7 matching, 0 mismatched. The manifest is truthful about what is on disk, so the next upgrade starts from a real record rather than repeating the baseline sweep.

Marker moved to 0.1.6. Exit code 0.

CRITERION 3 — THE 0.1.4 CASE: PASS. Sprint 6's seven permanent conflicts are gone. Installed published 0.1.4 untouched (no manifest), upgraded to 0.1.6: "Upgraded 0.1.4 -> 0.1.6", conflicts reported = 0 (sprint 6's live gate recorded seven, permanently), manifest populated with all 7 paths, sprint 3's standard present in qa1.md, exit code 0. The inert-in-the-field condition sprint 8 exists to fix is fixed.

CRITERION 4 — SPRINT 6'S SAFETY PROPERTY, THE NON-NEGOTIABLE REGRESSION CHECK: PASS.
Planted SENTINEL-S8-MUST-SURVIVE-OR-THIS-IS-A-FAIL in .claude/agents/qa1.md in a published-0.1.4 install, then upgraded to 0.1.6. The sentinel survived (grep count 1) and the file's sha256 was IDENTICAL before and after (84ebb0c247c83082 both sides). It was reported as a conflict. Baselines have not made the destructive branch reachable.

The manifest handling of that file is the detail worth recording: the target's manifest came out with SIX entries, not seven, and .claude/agents/qa1.md is absent from it. The edited file matched no baseline, so it was not proven untouched, so it was neither upgraded nor recorded. That is Req 3 behaving exactly as specified — we do not know what that file is, and it is not guessed at.

CRITERION 5 — BOTH CONFLICT MESSAGES, OBSERVED, EACH FROM ITS OWN REAL CONDITION: PASS.
Condition A, local edits AND upstream genuinely changed the file. Installed 0.1.2, edited qa1.md, upgraded to 0.1.6 (qa1.md really did change between those releases). Message, verbatim: "...This file's shipped content has changed since it was first published; to see exactly what's different in the current release, run `npx fully-completely` again inside an empty scratch directory to get a fresh copy, then diff it against your own file and merge anything you want by hand." Correct — upstream did move, and the reader is pointed at how to see it. My local edit survived.

Condition B, local edits and upstream did NOT change the file. The 0.1.4 sentinel target above. Message, verbatim: "...There's no upstream update pending for this file — if it looks different from what we'd install, that difference is entirely your own edit, not something we changed. Nothing to reconcile; no action needed unless you want one."

Read cold, B does not read as an alarm and does not send anyone to diff nothing. Neither message asserts that upstream moved unless upstream actually moved. This is the direct fix to the falsehood sprint 6 shipped, where all seven files got "Upstream has updated <file> since the version you have" and upstream had updated none of them. Sprint 6's Req 4 specified a claim; sprint 8's specifies a condition, and the difference is visible in the terminal.

CRITERION 6 — EXIT CODE 0 ON SUCCESS: PASS. Checked with the actual exit status, not inferred from absence of an error. Exit 0 observed on all five runs: fresh 0.1.6 install, 0.1.2 -> 0.1.6, 0.1.4 -> 0.1.6, the sentinel-conflict upgrade, and the edited-file upgrade. REQ 2 — THE BASELINE TABLE, REGENERATED RATHER THAN READ. THIS WAS THE HIGHEST-VALUE CHECK AVAILABLE TO ME.
A wrong hash in this table silently overwrites somebody's edited file, and reading the file cannot detect one. So I rebuilt it from the outside: fetched all six published tarballs (0.1.0, 0.1.1, 0.1.2, 0.1.3, 0.1.4, 0.1.5) with `npm pack`, extracted each, and recomputed the CRLF-normalised sha256 of all seven tracked paths in every version, comparing each against the committed table.

  VERIFIED MATCHING: 42     MISMATCHED: 0     MISSING: 0     TOTAL: 42

Every hash in the shipped baseline table corresponds to real published content. The table covers versions 0.1.0-0.1.5 and the seven user-owned paths, which is the complete set of prior releases. This was done independently of scripts/baselines/generate.js — I hashed the tarballs directly rather than re-running the project's own generator, so a bug in the generator would not have hidden from this check.

BASELINE DATA ACTUALLY SHIPS. QA1's concern was that .npmignore excluding the table would ship a feature that silently does nothing. It is present in the published tarball at package/scripts/baselines/user-owned-content.json. Worth noting for the next reader: it does NOT appear in an installed target, and that is correct, not a leak — install.js reads it via BASELINES_PATH = path.join(SOURCE_ROOT, 'scripts', 'baselines', ...), i.e. from the package it is running out of, never from the project it is installing into. My first sweep looked in the target, found nothing, and I chased it down before scoring rather than filing it.
